analysis.one_liner: Bans grocery stores and delivery apps from using shoppers' personal data to set individual prices.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2026 with one cosponsor, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and no vote has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop large grocery stores (15,000 square feet and up) and food delivery services from using a shopper's personal data to raise that shopper's price. It would also require online grocers to tell you when an item's availability changed or when the price depends on weight, require delivery services to get your approval before substituting an item, and let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the rules. It would also order a Labor Department report on whether electronic shelf labels affect grocery-store jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday grocery shoppers, especially people who shop online or through delivery apps. The bill would prevent stores from quietly charging one shopper more than another for the same food based on data about them, and it would stop delivery apps from swapping items into an order without the customer's okay.

how_it_helps.text: A covered entity — a food retailer of at least 15,000 square feet or a third-party delivery provider — may not use technology that applies a consumer's personal data to engage in dynamic pricing, defined as raising the price of food based on that consumer's data.

When selling groceries online, covered retailers must tell the customer if an item's availability has changed or if the item is weighed to set its price, and delivery providers must get the customer's explicit approval before substituting an item.
Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the Federal Trade Commission Act, so the FTC can enforce the ban with its existing penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Large grocery chains and delivery services, which would have to keep prices uniform rather than using personal data to raise individual prices, and would bear the cost of changing pricing systems and online-ordering software. The exception clause also raises the risk that stores shift data-driven price differences into loyalty programs.

drawbacks.text: The ban has large carve-outs: it does not apply to loyalty or membership program benefits, temporary discounts, offers a consumer consented to in exchange for data, or price differences based on objective costs like shipping and taxes — so retailers could still legally charge different prices through loyalty sign-ups and consent flows.
The rules only reach stores of at least 15,000 square feet, so smaller food retailers face no restriction on data-driven pricing.
Compliance would require changes to pricing and online-ordering systems at thousands of large stores, and some of that cost could show up in prices or fewer features for shoppers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — no charging a shopper more for groceries because of their data — is a straightforward consumer protection that most shoppers would want. The main weakness is design: the loyalty-program and consent exceptions leave a wide legal path for the same practice, and the 15,000-square-foot floor exempts smaller stores, so the protection is real but porous.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not acted on it, so nothing has been voted on yet.

narrative.text: Representative Josh Gottheimer introduced the bill on May 19, 2026, with Representative Mike Lawler joining, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
It has one cosponsor, a Republican, and no further action has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost; large grocers and delivery apps simply continue operating without the proposed pricing restrictions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No ruling yet; the bill is still parked in committee

for.name: Josh Gottheimer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it to the House floor

for.name: Mike Lawler
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor, making it a bipartisan pair

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat and a Republican introduced it together, but with only two members on board there is no record yet of broad support or organized opposition.

industries.industry: Large grocery chains (15,000 sq ft and up)
industries.note: The bill would bar them from using shopper data to raise individual prices and would add disclosure duties for online orders. Shoppers benefit from uniform, transparent prices; the chains lose a data-driven pricing tool.

They could no longer use personal data for dynamic pricing and would need explicit customer approval before substituting an item in an order. The substitution rule directly addresses a common delivery-app complaint.

industries.industry: Grocery technology and electronic shelf label makers
industries.note: The bill only orders a Labor Department report on whether electronic shelf labels affect grocery employment; it does not ban the labels. Widespread adoption could still proceed.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Energy and Commerce Committee with a single cosponsor and no committee activity since referral. Most bills at this stage never reach the floor, and without added cosponsors or committee action it is unlikely to become law this session.
